Within 60 days after the cutoff, there will be statements such as "Platform X lets people know what Country A doesn't want people to know" will appear in the public opinion about Leader A settling in Platform X and Country B, emphasizing that the platform has opened a hole in Country A's information control.

time.desc: The short video platform announced the implementation of stricter communication and advertising restrictions on state-affiliated media accounts with certain national backgrounds to reduce the chance of their content entering the recommendation stream.
Federal appeals court releases expedited hearing schedule and identifies key milestones in cases challenging strip-or-ban laws
The platform confirmed that it had encountered a zero-day vulnerability attack triggered by private messages and said it had taken measures to intercept and assist the victim's account recovery.

The government systematically responded to the platform lawsuit in court documents, emphasizing that measures such as data segregation are insufficient to eliminate national security risks and raising more specific charges.
Federal regulators jointly filed a children's privacy-related civil lawsuit against the platform and its parent company, alleging long-term illegal collection of minors' data
Platform formally files lawsuit challenging "stripping or ban" law and discloses its local data and moderation architecture to refute security accusations
The case surrounding the “strip or ban” law gets its first oral argument and enters the substantive stage at a federal appeals court
Several states and regions jointly sued the platform, accusing it of harming the physical and mental health of minors and misleading the public with addictive products and algorithm design.

The government of an allied country ordered the closure of the platform's local company operations based on the conclusion of the national security review. The platform stated that it would seek judicial relief.
The federal appeals court ruled to uphold the "stripping or banning" law, and the platform announced that it would continue to appeal to prevent the ban from taking effect.

After the unfavorable ruling, the platform submitted an emergency stay application to the court to request a delay in the implementation of the ban, and the government immediately submitted an objection.
Federal appeals court refuses to stay enforcement of "stripping or ban" law pending Supreme Court hearing, platforms say they will continue to appeal

The platform and its parent company filed an emergency petition with the Supreme Court seeking to prevent the ban from taking effect, while elected leaders publicly stated that they were studying the issue.

The Supreme Court announced that it would expedite the acceptance of relevant appeals and arranged a date for oral arguments, but it did not immediately order a suspension of the law from taking effect.
A presidential candidate officially joined the short video platform and posted his first video. The number of followers on his account exceeded millions within two days.

Intelligence officials publicly accused the platform in court documents for the first time of censoring overseas content and storing user data on offshore servers at the request of foreign governments.

The management department of the national legislative body announced that it will remove all applications owned by the parent company from its managed devices within a time limit, expanding the scope of the original ban.

The platform officially filed a lawsuit in court to challenge the divestment or ban law, and disclosed for the first time that its recommendation engine and user data are stored in the servers of domestic cloud service providers.
Institution B Submit documents to the court detailing Platform X specific allegations that pose a national security threat
Institution B and supervision Institution B filed a lawsuit against Platform X and its Parent Company Y for illegally collecting children’s personal information

Platform X started developing an independent version of Country A of its core algorithm in response to regulatory pressure from Agency Nine. It plans to rebuild a domestic independent copy of the recommendation engine and isolate Country A user data from Parent Company Y to alleviate data security concerns; this is seen as a technical compromise path outside of legal challenges, but whether it can be recognized by regulators is uncertain.
